author: Ahmed Ibrahim World Editor
title: IMF Sees Slower Global Trade Growth - Time News
text:
Global container shipping faces mounting pressure as the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects slower trade growth and shifting trade routes, with demand failing to keep pace with new vessel capacity, according to Sea-Intelligence.
The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook, analyzed by Sea-Intelligence, reveals that global trade volume growth is expected to moderate from 5.0% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2027, while import demand in advanced economies is forecast to slow from 5.0% in 2026 to 4.2% in 2027. This imbalance, as noted by Sea-Intelligence, means demand is not growing fast enough to absorb newly built vessel capacity, exacerbating supply-demand pressures in the container shipping sector.
Trade Growth Projections and Shipping Pressures
The IMF’s projections highlight a cumulative upward revision of 0.7 percentage point in global inflation, which is expected to rise to 4.7% in 2026 before easing to 4.1% in 2027. This trend, driven by energy and food prices, adds to the challenges facing the shipping industry. Sea-Intelligence warns that the slowing trade growth, combined with the influx of new containerships, is creating a critical mismatch. This means that demand is not growing fast enough to absorb all the newly built vessel capacity entering service,
the analysis states, citing the Sea-Intelligence Sunday Spotlight.
US-China Tariffs Reshape Trade Routes
New US-China tariffs introduced in 2025 have significantly altered global cargo flows. Chinese exports to the US fell by 22% over 12 months, while US exports to China dropped by 25%, according to Sea-Intelligence. However, overall trade volumes remained stable as production shifted to other markets. Chinese producers redirected 52% of their products to other Asian countries, while US exporters sent 17% of their goods to alternative destinations. This shift has complicated logistics networks, adding extra port calls and transportation costs for shippers.
The realignment of trade routes has forced container carriers to adapt their networks. Manufacturers now send components to countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia for assembly before exporting finished goods to the US. This strategy has kept trade volumes steady but increased operational complexity. The products are put together there and then shipped to the US,
Sea-Intelligence explains, noting the ripple effects on shipping lines.
AI Trade Boom and Shipping Implications
While trade in AI hardware has reached record levels relative to global GDP, the physical weight of these goods has increased only marginally. High-value components like microprocessors are typically transported by air, limiting their impact on ocean freight demand. However, the construction of AI data centers requires heavy materials and equipment, which are transported in ocean containers. This creates new cargo opportunities for shipping lines, as noted by Sea-Intelligence.
The AI boom underscores a broader trend: trade growth in high-value, low-volume goods is not translating directly into container demand. While the money spent on AI trade has grown a lot, the actual physical weight of these goods has barely grown,
the analysis states. This dynamic highlights the sector’s need to diversify its cargo base as traditional trade patterns evolve.
The shipping industry now faces a dual challenge: managing the slowdown in traditional trade growth while capitalizing on emerging sectors like AI infrastructure. With the IMF’s projections indicating continued pressure through 2027, carriers must balance fleet utilization with the shifting demands of global commerce.
